newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian debt holds up despite U.S. threat.
newsitem.headline: Australian debt holds up despite U.S. threat.

text.p: *The long end of the Australian debt market closed firm on Friday, despite fears of what impact the U.S. non-payroll report could bring to global debt markets next week.
*Local 10-year bond future sets new record of 93.695.
The long end of the Australian debt market closed firm despite concerns about the possible impact of the U.S. payrolls report on global markets early next week.

The 10-year bond futures contract struck a record high of 93.695 during the afternoon session, believing the recent rally can continue further based on current fundamentals and against a firm U.S. Treasury market back drop.
Local long-end yields are now standing at their lowest level since the early 1970s and will be looking to progress the rally further if next Thursday's labour force report proves weak.

Traders said offshore demand for long-dated, higher yielding semi-government bonds, ahead of the pricing of the A$1.0 billion Fannie Mae global 10-year bond later on Friday, also underpinned the market.
The Fannie Mae bond will be priced in London at 10 basis points over government debt.

The jury is still out over whether this week's 1/2 point cut in official rates to 5.0 percent by the Reserve Bank is the last in the cycle, but if data continues to remain weak, sentiment will push the rally on further.

The local yield curve continued to flatten after this week's rate cut induced steepening with the long end gaining most from the strength of the U.S. market. New Zealand debt was again undermined by the plight of the N.Z. dollar.
